source_note: Yoav Shoham and Kevin Leyton-Brown, Multiagent Systems: Algorithmic, Game-Theoretic, and Logical Foundations, Cambridge University Press, 2009. The local file is the authors' free electronic Revision 1.1 (2009, 2010), an uncorrected manuscript formatted differently from the printed book with different page numbering; the text itself states the printed book is definitive. PDF: books-must-have copy used, size 3914452 bytes, full sha256 f5d45b609914bcd71241da4e3fb8fd311d51a1fce52cb285a1ab245e4f829a84, book_id is the first 16 hex of the gatekeeper scan digest sha256(str(size) + bytes). A second copy of identical size sits in books-c-systems. Extracted text is large and generally clean (about 237k words) but the extraction breaks some words at line wraps, interleaves running heads and margin labels, and garbles some displayed mathematics; quotes were chosen from passages that are clean and contiguous in the text file, and equation primitives use only formulas whose content is stated legibly in the text. Page anchors cite book pages and sections as printed in this revision. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: Distributed CSP: each variable is owned by a different agent who decides its value with relative autonomy while communicating with constraint-graph neighbors
primitives.verbatim_quote: In a distributed CSP, each variable is owned by a different agent. The goal is still to find a global variable assignment that meets the constraints, but each agent decides on the value of his own variable with relative autonomy.
assumptions: Variables are partitioned one per agent
Agents communicate only with neighbors in the constraint graph
A global assignment must satisfy all constraints or be proven unsatisfiable
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks when the constraint graph is dense or communication is lossy; local views can cycle without nogood learning or a priority order

layer2.mapping: A game state decomposes into variables owned by different actors (units, position groups, coaching staffs); a feasible joint assignment is one where every pairwise constraint (matchup, health, scheme fit) is simultaneously satisfied, and infeasibility is a proved result, not a guess
layer2.telemetry: Per-variable state feeds: player availability, matchup assignments, scheme constraints, and neighbor messages between position groups

primitives.name: Asynchronous backtracking: agents under a priority order tentatively assign values, generate nogoods only from values already announced by higher agents, and communicate selectively
primitives.verbatim_quote: Here, agents make tentative choices of a value for their variables, only generate Nogoods that incorporate values already generated by the agents above them in the order
assumptions: A total priority ordering on agents exists
Agents act asynchronously and messages are eventually delivered
Nogoods are sound: they record genuinely forbidden combinations
primitives.breakdown_regime: Worst case is exponential in problem size; message delays and stale agent views can cause redundant search, and completeness depends on nogood retention

layer2.mapping: When a candidate joint plan fails, the engine records the minimal conflicting partial assignment as a nogood and backtracks only the lowest priority component that caused the conflict, instead of discarding the whole plan
layer2.telemetry: Search telemetry: tentative assignments, conflict sets, nogood store size, and backtrack counts per variable

primitives.name: Asynchronous dynamic programming for path planning: one process per node repeatedly relaxes distance estimates h(i) toward the min over neighbors until h converges to the true shortest-path values
primitives.verbatim_quote: The h values are initialized to ∞, and incrementally decrease to their correct values.
primitives.latex: h(i) \leftarrow \min_j f(j), \quad f(j) = w(i, j) + h(j)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.h(i): current distance estimate at node i, in path-cost units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w(i, j): edge weight from node i to neighbor j, in path-cost units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f(j): candidate distance through neighbor j, in path-cost units

assumptions: Graph with nonnegative edge weights w
One process or agent per node
Estimates start at infinity and only decrease
primitives.breakdown_regime: Convergence can require one step per node on the shortest path and is impractical when the state space cannot be enumerated; the heuristic single-agent variant trades guarantees for reach

layer2.mapping: Drive charts, field position progressions, and win probability surfaces are shortest path and cost-to-go surfaces; asynchronous relaxation lets local estimates (per down, distance, and field zone) update from neighbor values without a global synchronous sweep
layer2.telemetry: Play by play state transitions, yards and cost per transition, and per-node estimate revision counts

primitives.name: Utility function: a mapping from states of the world to real numbers; under uncertainty an agent's utility is the expected value of that function over the probability distribution on states
primitives.verbatim_quote: When the agent is uncertain about which state of the world he faces, his utility is defined as the expected value of his utility function with respect to the appropriate probability distribution over states.
assumptions: Agent preferences satisfy the utility theoretic axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence)
A probability distribution over states is available
Utility numbers are comparable across states for the same agent
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when preferences are incomplete, intransitive, or not representable by a real valued function; interpersonal comparison of utility is not licensed by the theory

layer2.mapping: Every actor in a matchup (quarterback, coordinator, kicker) is scored on a single numeric scale per state of the game, and choice under uncertainty is expectation over that scale, which is what lets the engine trade off plays with different risk profiles on one axis
layer2.telemetry: Outcome distributions per decision: play results, drive outcomes, and the utility scale calibration from historical preferences

primitives.name: Normal-form game: a tuple (N, A, u) with a finite set of players, a product set of action profiles, and a utility function per player
primitives.verbatim_quote: Definition 3.2.1 (Normal-form game) A (finite, n-person) normal-form game is a tuple (N, A, u), where:
assumptions: Finite player set and finite action sets
Players choose simultaneously or without observing others' choices
Payoffs are common knowledge in the basic model
primitives.breakdown_regime: The representation grows exponentially in the number of players and actions and hides timing, information, and repetition structure that richer forms expose

layer2.mapping: A single snap, a play call duel, or a fourth down decision is a normal-form object: two or more actors, a finite menu of calls, and a payoff (expected points or win probability change) for every combination, which the engine can enumerate and audit cell by cell
layer2.telemetry: Play call menus per situation, payoff matrix entries from the projection model, and the situation identifiers that index each game

primitives.name: Pareto optimality: a strategy profile is Pareto optimal if no other profile Pareto dominates it by making some player better off and no player worse off
primitives.verbatim_quote: if there does not exist another strategy profile s′ ∈ S that Pareto dominates s
assumptions: Utilities of all players are defined on the same set of profiles
Dominance requires weak improvement for all and strict improvement for at least one player
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pareto optimality is silent about fairness and about which optimal profile obtains; many profiles can be Pareto optimal while being terrible for some player

layer2.mapping: Candidate game plans are screened for dominated plans first: a plan that is no better on any objective (expected points, win probability, injury risk exposure) and worse on one is removed before equilibrium reasoning begins
layer2.telemetry: Multi objective plan scores: expected points, win probability delta, turnover risk, and player workload per candidate plan

primitives.name: Best response: a strategy maximizing a player's utility given the others' strategies; when its support has two or more actions the player is indifferent among them
primitives.verbatim_quote: When the support of a best response s∗ includes two or more actions, the agent must be indifferent among them-otherwise, the agent would prefer to reduce the probability of playing at least one of the actions to zero.
assumptions: The other players' strategy profile is held fixed
The player can evaluate expected utility for every own strategy
primitives.breakdown_regime: Best responses need not be unique; against a moving opponent the best response chases a moving target and need not converge

layer2.mapping: Each side's play calling is evaluated as a response function: given the opponent's tendencies, which call maximizes expected value, and where the opponent is indifferent between calls is exactly where tendency data loses discriminating power
layer2.telemetry: Opponent tendency distributions by situation and the payoff of each candidate call against them

primitives.name: Nash equilibrium: a strategy profile in which every player's strategy is a best response to the others, so no agent wants to deviate unilaterally
primitives.verbatim_quote: Intuitively, a Nash equilibrium is a stable strategy profile: no agent would want to change his strategy if he knew what strategies the other agents were following.
primitives.latex: u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}) \geq u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) \quad \forall s_i \in S_i

symbol_and_unit_ledger.u_i: player i utility, in utility units

assumptions: Each player knows the others' strategies at the candidate profile
Deviations are unilateral only
Expected utility is the evaluation criterion
primitives.breakdown_regime: Equilibria can be multiple, Pareto inferior, or require mixing that real actors do not perform; existence says nothing about selection

layer2.mapping: A stable play calling pattern is one where neither coordinator gains by unilaterally changing call mix given the other's mix; the engine reports these fixed points as the baseline expectation before layering situation specific deviations
layer2.telemetry: Call mix frequencies per side, payoff per call pairing, and unilateral deviation gains computed per situation

primitives.name: Nash's theorem: every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies (Theorem 3.3.22, Nash 1951)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 3.3.22 (Nash, 1951) Every game with a finite number of players and action profiles has at least one Nash equilibrium.
assumptions: Finite number of players
Finite action sets, with mixed strategies forming a compact convex set
Continuous payoff functions in the mixed extension
primitives.breakdown_regime: The theorem is nonconstructive about selection and the equilibrium may be fully mixed; computing one is PPAD-hard in general, and infinite or discontinuous games can lack equilibria

layer2.mapping: Existence licenses the engine to always search for a mixed strategy fixed point in finite matchup models instead of reporting no solution; when actors are restricted to pure strategies the guarantee lapses and the engine must say so
layer2.telemetry: Game size metadata: player count, action counts, and solver convergence flags per modeled interaction

primitives.name: Minimax theorem (von Neumann 1928): in a finite two-player zero-sum game, every Nash equilibrium gives each player exactly his maxmin value and his minmax value
primitives.verbatim_quote: in any Nash equilibrium5 each player receives a payoff that is equal to both his maxmin value and his minmax value
assumptions: Two players
Zero-sum payoffs
Finite game with mixed strategies allowed
primitives.breakdown_regime: The equality collapses outside zero-sum two-player settings; in general-sum games maxmin is only a security level, not an equilibrium payoff

layer2.mapping: In strictly opposed subproblems (offense gains exactly what defense loses, as in expected points on a single play) the engine can price a call by its security level, the value guaranteed regardless of the opponent's response
layer2.telemetry: Zero-sum subgame payoffs, security level computations, and the gap between equilibrium value and maxmin value per subgame

primitives.name: Dominated strategy: a strategy is strictly (weakly, very weakly) dominated if another strategy does at least as well (better) against every opponent profile; iterated removal prunes the game
primitives.verbatim_quote: A strategy si is strictly (weakly; very weakly) dominated dominated for an agent i if some other strategy s′i strictly (weakly; very weakly) strategy dominates si .
assumptions: Payoff comparisons hold against all opponent profiles
For strict dominance, iterated removal order does not matter
Players are rational and this is mutually known for the iterated argument
primitives.breakdown_regime: Weak dominance removal is order dependent and can delete Nash equilibria; dominance by mixed strategies requires solving for the dominating mixture

layer2.mapping: Play calls that are worse than another call against every defensive look are pruned from the recommendation set with the dominating call recorded, which keeps the reasoning trail auditable
layer2.telemetry: Per-call payoff vectors across opponent looks and the dominance certificates naming the dominating alternative

primitives.name: Rationalizability: a strategy is rationalizable if it is a best response to some belief about rational opponents, recursively; rationalizable strategies are what perfect rationality alone justifies
primitives.verbatim_quote: Informally, a strategy profile for player i is rationalizable if it is a best response to some beliefs that i could have about the strategies that the other players will take.
assumptions: Players are perfectly rational
Rationality is common belief, iterated
Beliefs over opponent strategies are unrestricted probability distributions
primitives.breakdown_regime: The rationalizable set can be large and uninformative in games with many strategies; it disciplines beliefs but rarely selects a unique prediction

layer2.mapping: The engine keeps any opponent call that a rational coordinator could justify given some belief, and only discards calls that no belief justifies, which prevents overconfident narrowing of the opponent's menu
layer2.telemetry: Belief sets over opponent calls and best response justifications logged per retained call

primitives.name: Correlated equilibrium: a tuple (v, pi, sigma) where a shared random device privately recommends actions and no agent gains by remapping his recommendation through any alternative mapping
primitives.verbatim_quote: a correlated equilibrium is a tuple (v, π, σ), where v is a tuple of random variables

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\pi(d): probability of device outcome profile d, dimensionless probability
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u_i: player i utility, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\sigma_i: mapping from player i private signal to his action

assumptions: A correlation device draws from a joint distribution pi
Each agent sees only his own component of the draw
Agents evaluate deviations as remappings of their own signal
primitives.breakdown_regime: Requires a trusted or commonly observed correlation source; without one the concept reduces toward Nash, and the set can be large

layer2.mapping: Shared public signals (weather, officiating crew tendencies, injury news timing) correlate both sides' behavior; the engine models recommendations from such signals and checks that neither side profits by systematically ignoring the signal
layer2.telemetry: Public signal streams, conditional call distributions given each signal, and deviation gains per remapping

primitives.name: Extensive-form games: a finite representation (game tree) that does not assume players act simultaneously, with choice nodes, a player function, and information structure
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this chapter we will look at extensive-form games, a finite representation that does not always assume that players act simultaneously.
assumptions: Finite tree of choice and terminal nodes
A player function assigns each choice node to a player
Perfect information version: each player observes all prior moves
primitives.breakdown_regime: Trees explode combinatorially with horizon and branching; the perfect information version misrepresents simultaneous or hidden moves, which need information sets

layer2.mapping: A drive is a game tree: sequence of downs, calls, and responses with terminal payoffs; the engine reasons over the tree rather than a flat matrix whenever move order and observed responses matter
layer2.telemetry: Drive state trees: down, distance, field position, call, response, and terminal outcome per path

primitives.name: Subgame and subgame-perfect equilibrium: a subgame is the restriction of the game to the descendants of a node; an SPE is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, eliminating noncredible threats
primitives.verbatim_quote: Definition 5.1.4 (Subgame) Given a perfect-information extensive-form game G, the subgame of G rooted at node h is the restriction of G to the descendants of h.
assumptions: Perfect information
Subgames are well defined at every node in the perfect information case
Players are sequentially rational
primitives.breakdown_regime: With imperfect information, subgames in this sense may not exist at most nodes and SPE loses bite; the refinement also assumes rational play at nodes reached only after mistakes

layer2.mapping: Late game decisions are audited subgame by subgame: a strategy that looks optimal from kickoff but is irrational at the node actually reached (for example a threat to keep passing while protecting a lead) is vetoed
layer2.telemetry: Node level strategy evaluations, subgame boundaries in drive trees, and credibility flags on off-path threats

primitives.name: Folk theorem for infinitely repeated games: equilibrium average payoffs are exactly the feasible payoffs that give each player at least his minmax payoff, sustained by punishment strategies
primitives.verbatim_quote: Roughly speaking, it states that in an infinitely repeated game the set of average rewards attainable in equilibrium are precisely those pairs attainable under mixed strategies in a single-stage game, with the constraint on the mixed strategies that each player's payoff is at least the amount he would receive if the other players adopted minmax strategies against him.
assumptions: The stage game repeats infinitely (or with no known end)
Players discount the future sufficiently little
Deviations are observable so punishments can be triggered
primitives.breakdown_regime: With a known finite horizon the argument unravels by backward induction; imperfect monitoring weakens the punishments that sustain cooperation

layer2.mapping: Divisional rivals meet repeatedly across seasons, so the engine treats one game as a stage in a repeated interaction: tendencies shown now change future meetings, and restraint or exploitation today is priced against future responses
layer2.telemetry: Head to head history across seasons, tendency carryover between meetings, and discounting by time between matchups

primitives.name: Stochastic game (Markov game): a tuple (Q, N, A, P, r) where a collection of stage games is linked by action dependent state transitions; an MDP is the one-player special case
primitives.verbatim_quote: An MDP is simply a stochastic game with only one player, while a repeated game is a stochastic game in which there is only one stage game.
assumptions: Finite state set and finite action sets
Transition probabilities depend on state and joint action
Payoff functions are defined per state and action profile
primitives.breakdown_regime: Equilibrium computation is far harder than for MDPs; stationary equilibria may fail to exist in some undiscounted settings, and the state space grows with game detail

layer2.mapping: A football game is a stochastic game, not a sequence of independent snaps: the state (score, clock, field position, fatigue) transitions under both teams' actions, and the engine evaluates calls by their effect on the whole state trajectory
layer2.telemetry: State transition logs per snap, state dependent payoff tables, and fatigue or personnel state variables

primitives.name: Bayesian games: games of incomplete information where players are uncertain about the very game being played, represented by a common prior over games and private information partitions
primitives.verbatim_quote: In contrast, Bayesian games, or games of incomplete information, allow us to represent players' uncertainties about the very game being played.
assumptions: All possible games share the player set and strategy spaces and differ in payoffs
Beliefs are posteriors from conditioning a common prior on private signals
The game structure itself (not the realized type) is common knowledge
primitives.breakdown_regime: The common prior assumption is substantive and often false in practice; type spaces can be enormous, and misspecified priors corrupt every downstream equilibrium

layer2.mapping: Injury status, a quarterback's true health, and a coordinator's game plan are types: the engine maintains a prior over opponent types, updates it from signals (practice reports, early plays), and solves for behavior per type rather than pretending certainty
layer2.telemetry: Type priors per opponent, signal likelihoods (reports, snap counts, early tendencies), and posterior updates during the game

primitives.name: Congestion game: each player chooses a subset of resources and each resource's cost depends on how many agents select it, so utility is driven by crowding
primitives.verbatim_quote: Intuitively, in a congestion game each player chooses some subset from a set of resources, and the cost of each resource depends on the number of other agents who select it.
assumptions: Finite resource set
Costs depend only on the number of users of each resource (anonymity)
Utility is the negative sum of chosen resource costs
primitives.breakdown_regime: Real settings add identity dependent costs and capacities that break anonymity; computing equilibria in succinct variants can still be hard

layer2.mapping: Defensive attention is a congestible resource: when every defense crowds the same receiver or run fit, the marginal value of attacking elsewhere rises; the engine prices targets by how crowded the coverage resource already is
layer2.telemetry: Coverage and attention counts per receiver or gap, target shares, and the marginal cost curve as crowding increases

primitives.name: Potential game: a game admitting a potential function whose change under any unilateral deviation equals the deviator's utility change; every finite potential game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 6.4.5 Every (finite) potential game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.u_i: player i utility, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi: potential function over action profiles, in utility units

assumptions: An exact potential function exists for the game
The game is finite
Deviations are unilateral
primitives.breakdown_regime: Most games are not potential games; best response dynamics converge only within this class and weighted or ordinal variants weaken the conclusions

layer2.mapping: When a subproblem can be written with a potential (for example total field position value across a drive), the engine knows pure equilibria exist and that simple best response iteration converges, so it can certify the result instead of sampling blindly
layer2.telemetry: Potential function values per profile, best response step traces, and convergence certificates per subproblem

primitives.name: Price of anarchy: the ratio of social cost at selfish equilibrium to optimal social cost, measuring how much efficiency is lost to self-interested behavior
primitives.verbatim_quote: Intuitively, the price of anarchy is the proportion of additional social cost that is incurred because of agents' self-interested behavior.
assumptions: A social cost function over profiles is defined
Equilibria of the selfish game exist
An optimal (centrally chosen) profile is well defined for comparison
primitives.breakdown_regime: The ratio is a worst case measure and can overstate typical loss; it depends entirely on the chosen social cost function

layer2.mapping: The engine audits the gap between what self-interested play calling produces and what a coordinated optimum would produce, so it can report how much of a projected edge is structural and how much is lost to predictable selfish tendencies
layer2.telemetry: Equilibrium social cost versus coordinated optimum per modeled system, reported as a ratio with its cost definition

primitives.name: Fictitious play: each agent believes the opponent plays the empirical distribution of his past actions and best responds to that belief
primitives.verbatim_quote: if A is the set of the opponent's actions, and for every a ∈ A we let w(a) be the number of times that the opponent has played action a

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(a): assessed probability that the opponent plays action a, dimensionless probability
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w(a): count of past plays of action a, in observations

assumptions: Play is repeated against a stationary opponent
Full history of opponent actions is observed
Agents best respond to the empirical frequency belief
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails against adaptive or deceptive opponents and in games where empirical frequencies cycle; convergence to equilibrium is guaranteed only in special classes such as zero-sum and potential games

layer2.mapping: Tendency modeling is fictitious play with discipline: the engine forms beliefs from the opponent's counted past calls and best responds, while tracking whether the opponent is stationary enough for those frequencies to mean anything
layer2.telemetry: Opponent action counts by situation, empirical frequency vectors, and stationarity diagnostics over time windows

primitives.name: No-regret learning: a rule exhibits no regret if, for every fixed strategy in hindsight, the probability that long-run regret stays positive is zero; no-regret play converges to correlated equilibrium
primitives.verbatim_quote: Definition 7.5.2 (No-regret learning rule) A learning rule exhibits no regret if for any pure strategy of the agent s it holds that P r([lim inf Rt (s)] ≤ 0) = 1.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.R_t(s): regret at time t for not having played s, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\alpha_t: agent's average payoff received up to time t, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\alpha_t(s): average payoff the agent would have received by always playing s, in utility units

assumptions: The comparison class is fixed strategies played throughout
Other agents' behavior is taken as it occurred (no counterfactual response)
The horizon grows without bound for the asymptotic statement
primitives.breakdown_regime: No regret is an asymptotic, worst case guarantee; finite horizon regret can still be large, and the benchmark ignores strategies that adapt

layer2.mapping: The engine grades its own recommendation rules by hindsight regret per situation: if a fixed simple rule would have beaten the engine's choices over a season of similar spots, that is a measured defect to repair, not an opinion
layer2.telemetry: Per-situation decision logs, realized payoffs, and hindsight payoffs of benchmark fixed rules

primitives.name: Replicator dynamic: population shares of actions grow in proportion to their excess payoff over the population average, a continuous-time model of imitation and selection
primitives.verbatim_quote: The question is whether the process converges to a fixed proportion of the various pure strategies within the population, and if so to which fixed proportions.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\theta_t(a): population share playing action a at time t, dimensionless fraction
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u_t(a): expected payoff of action a at time t, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u_t^*: population average expected payoff at time t, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\dot{\\theta}_t(a): rate of change of the share, per unit time

assumptions: Large population with random matching
Payoff is fitness: reproduction or imitation is proportional to it
Continuous time approximation of frequent interaction
primitives.breakdown_regime: Shares of unplayed actions can never enter without mutation; finite populations add drift, and the dynamic need not converge in games with cycles

layer2.mapping: League wide scheme adoption follows replicator logic: concepts that outperform the league average spread from team to team each offseason, so the engine projects next season's tendency mix from this season's excess success per concept
layer2.telemetry: League wide usage shares per scheme or concept, success rates per concept, and season over season share changes

primitives.name: Evolutionarily stable strategy: a mixed strategy that resists invasion, earning more against the post-invasion mixture than any small invading strategy earns against it
primitives.verbatim_quote: Roughly speaking, an evolutionarily stable strategy is a mixed strategy that is "resistant to invasion" by new strategies.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.u: payoff function of the symmetric game, in utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\epsilon: invader population share, dimensionless small fraction

assumptions: Symmetric two-player game
Invading share epsilon is small
Payoffs are fitness in a large population
primitives.breakdown_regime: An ESS need not exist in a given game; the concept is static and silent about how the population reaches the strategy

layer2.mapping: A game plan tendency is treated as stable only if a small dose of a new concept cannot outperform it on its own terms; this is the engine's test for whether an opponent's established identity will survive contact with a novel wrinkle
layer2.telemetry: Incumbent tendency performance versus invading concept performance at small usage shares, per opponent

primitives.name: Signaling game: Nature selects a game by a known distribution, the informed player 1 acts, and player 2 responds without knowing Nature's choice but seeing player 1's action, so actions carry information
primitives.verbatim_quote: Definition 8.2.1 (Signaling game) A signaling game is a two-player game in which Nature selects a game to be played according to a commonly known distribution, player 1 is informed of that choice and chooses an action, and player 2 then chooses an action without knowing Nature's choice, but knowing player 1's choice.
assumptions: Two players, one informed of Nature's draw
The distribution over games is commonly known
The uninformed player observes the informed player's action before moving
primitives.breakdown_regime: Equilibria can be pooling (uninformative) or separating depending on incentives; cheap talk without payoff consequences can collapse to a babbling equilibrium where messages are ignored

layer2.mapping: Pre-snap signals are signaling games: formation, motion, and personnel tell the defense about the offense's type, and the engine evaluates whether a signal is credible (separating) or noise (pooling) from the incentives of the sender
layer2.telemetry: Signal to type conditional frequencies, defensive responses per signal, and payoff differences that make a signal credible or cheap

primitives.name: Arrow's theorem: with at least three outcomes, any social welfare function that is Pareto efficient and independent of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 9.4.4 (Arrow, 1951) If |O| ≥ 3, any social welfare function W that is Pareto efficient and independent of irrelevant alternatives is dictatorial.
assumptions: At least three outcomes
Finite voter set
Unrestricted domain of preference profiles
The function must satisfy Pareto efficiency and independence of irrelevant alternatives
primitives.breakdown_regime: The impossibility is escaped by restricting the domain (for example single-peaked preferences), enriching ballots to two-level approval as in ranking systems, or dropping one of the axioms

layer2.mapping: Aggregating many model voters (metrics, film grades, market signals) into one ranking cannot satisfy every fairness axiom at once; the engine therefore documents which axiom its aggregation knowingly relaxes instead of pretending the ranking is neutral
layer2.telemetry: Voter level rankings per signal family, aggregation rule configuration, and axiom violation reports per ranking

primitives.name: Revelation principle: any mechanism outcome can be replicated by a direct truthful mechanism, so mechanism design can restrict attention to mechanisms where agents reveal their true types
primitives.verbatim_quote: It means that, while one might have thought a priori that a particular mechanism design problem calls for an arbitrarily complex strategy space, in fact one can restrict one's attention to truthful, direct mechanisms.
assumptions: The original mechanism implements the outcome in the stated equilibrium concept
The designer can commit to the new mechanism
Agents' type spaces are well defined
primitives.breakdown_regime: The principle is an existence result, not a practicality result: the direct mechanism may be computationally intractable or require reporting an enormous type

layer2.mapping: When the engine designs an elicitation (what a team's revealed preferences over plays say about its private information), it can assume without loss that reports are truthful types and fold any strategic shading into the mechanism itself
layer2.telemetry: Report spaces per elicitation, implemented outcome mappings, and incentive compatibility checks per type

primitives.name: Groves mechanisms and VCG: efficient allocation with payments equal to a term depending only on others' reports minus the others' total value, with the Clarke tax setting that term to the others' welfare at the allocation chosen without the agent
primitives.verbatim_quote: The second-price auction is a special case of the VCG mechanism, and hence of the Groves mechanism.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\wp_i: payment charged to agent i, in currency or utility units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.h_i: term depending only on the other agents' reports, in the same units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{v}_j: reported valuation of agent j, in the same units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{v}_{-i}: reports of all agents except i

assumptions: Quasilinear preferences (utility is value minus payment)
The allocation rule maximizes total reported value
Agents report valuations to a direct mechanism
primitives.breakdown_regime: VCG is generally not budget balanced, is vulnerable to collusion and false-name bids, and needs the winner determination problem solved exactly to keep its guarantees

layer2.mapping: Externality pricing is the transferable core: a player's true cost to a lineup or a play is the welfare the rest of the system loses by his presence, which is how the engine prices a high usage player against the opportunities he displaces
layer2.telemetry: Counterfactual system value with and without each component, reported value tables, and displacement costs per component

primitives.name: Revenue equivalence theorem: under risk neutrality and independent private values, all efficient auctions in which the lowest type earns zero yield the same expected revenue and the same expected payments per type
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thus, when bidders are risk neutral and have independent private valuations, all the auctions we have spoken about so far-English, Japanese, Dutch, and all sealed bid auction protocols-are revenue equivalent.
assumptions: Risk-neutral bidders
Independent private values drawn from a common strictly increasing atomless distribution
The mechanism is efficient and the lowest valuation type has expected utility zero
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks with risk aversion, correlated or common values, asymmetry, or inefficient allocation rules; it equates revenue, not variance or simplicity

layer2.mapping: Equivalence results discipline comparison work: when two evaluation protocols satisfy the same invariance conditions, the engine expects identical headline numbers and investigates any gap as a bug or a violated condition rather than a discovery
layer2.telemetry: Protocol comparison tables, condition checklists per protocol, and payment or score identities across formats

primitives.name: Coalitional game with transferable utility: a pair (N, v) where the characteristic function v assigns every coalition a real-valued worth its members can distribute among themselves
primitives.verbatim_quote: v : 2N 7→ R associates with each coalition S ⊆ N a real-valued payoff v(S) that the coalition's members can distribute among themselves.
assumptions: Transferable utility: payoff is a single divisible quantity
v of the empty set is zero
A coalition's worth does not depend on how outsiders organize (the characteristic function form)
primitives.breakdown_regime: The form fails when outsiders' behavior affects a coalition's worth (partition function games) or when utility is not transferable

layer2.mapping: Units and position groups are coalitions with a joint worth (drive success with this personnel grouping) that must be divided into individual credit; the engine stores grouping worth first and argues about division second
layer2.telemetry: Grouping level outcome values for every personnel combination observed, with sample sizes per coalition

primitives.name: Shapley value: the unique efficient payoff division satisfying symmetry, dummy player, and additivity, equal to each player's average marginal contribution over all orderings of the grand coalition
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 12.2.7 Given a coalitional game (N, v), there is a unique pre-imputation φ(N, v) = φ(N, v) that satisfies the Symmetry, Dummy player, Additivity axioms.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\phi_i: Shapley payoff of player i, in the game's payoff units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v(S): worth of coalition S, in payoff units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.|S|: size of coalition S, dimensionless count
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v(S \\cup \\{i\\}) - v(S): marginal contribution of i to S, in payoff units

assumptions: Transferable utility coalitional game
The division must be a pre-imputation (feasible and efficient)
The three axioms are accepted as the fairness criteria
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact computation is exponential in the number of players without compact structure; the axioms are normative choices, and the value can violate individual rationality in nonconvex games

layer2.mapping: Player valuation is done the Shapley way: a player's worth is his average marginal contribution across the lineups he could join, not his raw totals, which is the engine's antidote to crediting a player for value his teammates created
layer2.telemetry: Lineup level worth tables, marginal contribution samples per player, and ordering based estimates with convergence bounds

primitives.name: The core: payoff vectors where every coalition receives at least its own worth, so no sub-coalition has an incentive to break away from the grand coalition
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thus, a payoff is in the core if and only if no sub-coalition has an incentive to break away from the grand coalition and share the payoff it is able to obtain independently.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_i: payoff allocated to player i, in payoff units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v(S): worth of coalition S, in payoff units

assumptions: Payoff vectors are imputations (efficient and individually rational)
Coalitions can credibly form and split their worth
Transferable utility
primitives.breakdown_regime: The core can be empty, in which case no stable division exists; when it is large it underdetermines the division and needs refinements such as the nucleolus

layer2.mapping: A credit division is accepted only if no subgroup (an offensive line unit, a receiver group) is shortchanged below what it produces on its own; core violations flag exactly which coalition the division is unfair to
layer2.telemetry: Coalition worth table, proposed credit allocations, and per-coalition shortfall checks

primitives.name: Partition model of knowledge: an agent's information is a partition of the possible worlds; the agent knows a sentence if it is true in every world in his partition cell
primitives.verbatim_quote: Definition 13.1.1 (Partition model) An (n-agent) partition model over a language Σ is a tuple A = (W, π, I1 , . . . , In ), where
assumptions: A well defined set of possible worlds W
Each agent's information partition is a true partition (disjoint cells covering W)
The interpretation function fixes which sentences are true in which worlds
primitives.breakdown_regime: The model imposes logical omniscience and perfect introspection (the S5 properties), which real agents violate; partitions also cannot express graded uncertainty without the probability extension

layer2.mapping: What a defense can distinguish from its film study is a partition over possible offensive game plans: two plans in the same cell are indistinguishable to that defense, and the engine only credits an actor with knowledge that is constant across his cell
layer2.telemetry: Indistinguishability classes per actor over game plan hypotheses, observation histories, and cell level knowledge checks

primitives.name: Common knowledge: a sentence is common knowledge in a group if everybody knows it and everybody knows that it is common knowledge, the fixed point of the everyone-knows operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: In other words, a sentence is common knowledge if everybody knows it and knows that it is common knowledge.
assumptions: A group of agents with knowledge operators over a shared structure
The fixed point (infinite iteration of everyone knows) is well defined
Agents reason about each other's knowledge without bound
primitives.breakdown_regime: True common knowledge is unattainable over unreliable channels (the coordinated attack problem); practical systems substitute high finite levels of mutual knowledge

layer2.mapping: The engine distinguishes what is merely true from what is common knowledge on the field: a tendency both sides know, and know the other knows, changes equilibrium play, while a one sided scouting fact changes only the holder's decisions
layer2.telemetry: Knowledge level annotations per fact (private, mutual, common), public announcement logs, and equilibrium shifts after public events

reasoning_traces.think: The book is a single architecture for reasoning about many self interested actors at once, and its order of construction matters. It begins with the case where the actors share one goal: distributed constraint satisfaction and distributed optimization. There the problem is coordination without conflict, and the tools are message passing, nogoods, priority orders, and asynchronous relaxation of value estimates. Even in this friendly setting the book is careful: a global solution is assembled from local views, correctness is a theorem about the protocol rather than a hope, and the price of distribution is measured in messages and convergence steps. This cooperative core is the part most readers skip, but for a reasoning engine it is foundational, because it shows how a joint assignment or a shortest path can be computed by the very actors who own the variables, with proofs that the distributed process lands on the same answer a central solver would give. Game theory then removes the shared goal. The normal form strips an interaction to players, actions, and utilities, and the book builds its solution concepts in layers of increasing epistemic demand. Pareto optimality asks only for joint efficiency. Best response and Nash equilibrium ask for mutual consistency of choices. Dominance and rationalizability ask what rationality alone, iterated as common belief, can justify. Correlated equilibrium adds a shared signal and shows that coordination on public randomness enlarges the stable set. The extensive form restores time and information, and with it subgame perfection and sequential equilibrium, which veto strategies that rely on threats no rational actor would carry out. Repeated, stochastic, Bayesian, congestion, and graphical games are then presented as controlled enrichments: add repetition and the folk theorem explodes the equilibrium set; add state transitions and the game becomes a Markov game whose one player limit is an MDP; add types and private signals and beliefs become part of the state; add resource crowding and a potential function restores pure equilibria and convergence. Learning is treated as the dynamic counterpart of equilibrium. Fictitious play forms beliefs from counted history, no regret rules guarantee that hindsight will not condemn the learner, and the replicator dynamic replaces deliberation with selection, tying Nash equilibrium to steady states and evolutionary stability to resistance against invasion. Communication gets its own analysis because talk is not free of strategy: cheap talk can collapse into babbling, while signaling games show when an action credibly transmits private information. Social choice and mechanism design then invert the problem. Instead of predicting behavior in a given game, the designer chooses the game. Arrow's theorem warns that aggregating preferences has no universally fair solution, while the revelation principle and the Groves and VCG mechanisms show how much can still be achieved: restrict attention to truthful direct mechanisms, price each actor his externality, and dominant strategy honesty follows. Auctions instantiate the theory and revenue equivalence shows that superficially different protocols collapse to the same expected payments under stated conditions. Coalitional theory finally asks how groups form and divide joint worth, answering with the Shapley value's axioms and the core's stability inequalities. The closing chapters on knowledge formalize the epistemic substrate everything else assumed: partitions of possible worlds, knowledge operators, and common knowledge as a fixed point, without which coordination results cannot even be stated precisely. Two further strands deserve emphasis because they decide whether the rest is usable in practice. The first is computation. The book never lets a solution concept float free of the cost of finding it: Nash equilibria of zero-sum games fall to linear programming, general two-player equilibria lead to linear complementarity and support enumeration, correlated equilibria return to linear programming, and computing equilibria or winner determination in richer representations is repeatedly shown to be hard in the worst case. An engine built on this book therefore budgets its reasoning, choosing representations, such as congestion or graphical structure, where the interaction graph is sparse enough for the wanted computation to finish, and reporting honestly when the exact object is out of reach and only an approximation with a stated error is available. The second strand is that communication and knowledge are modeled, not assumed. Speech acts, cheap talk, and signaling are analyzed with the same incentive tools as actions, because a message is a move in a game. Knowledge is given a semantics in partitioned possible worlds, belief is separated from knowledge, and belief revision is treated as an operation with its own postulates. An engine that ingests reports, rumors, and announcements needs exactly this: a way to represent who could distinguish which states, what an announcement changes when it is public, and why the same sentence can be informative from one sender and babbling from another. For a reasoning engine the transfer is direct. Most real prediction problems are multi actor: the outcome is produced by actors who observe different information, hold different objectives, and adapt to each other. The book supplies the checks such an engine needs. Is the candidate solution merely efficient, or is it a best response for every actor? Does it survive iterated dominance? Does it rely on a threat that fails in the subgame where it would be executed? Is the actor's information a partition cell, a type drawn from a prior, or common knowledge? Is the learning rule that produced the tendency data no regret, fictitious play, or mere imitation, and what does each imply about where the data will drift? Where the engine aggregates many signals into one ranking, Arrow's theorem forces it to declare which fairness property it is giving up. Where it assigns credit to members of a unit, Shapley and the core give the fairness axioms and the stability test. Where it prices a component, VCG gives the externality definition. None of this is metaphor: each primitive carries assumptions that can be checked against telemetry, and a breakdown regime that names exactly when the machinery stops applying. The engine that internalizes this book stops asking only what will happen and starts asking what each actor, knowing what he knows and wanting what he wants, can rationally do, and whether the joint result is stable, efficient, learnable, and fair by stated criteria.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from von Neumann's minimax theorem and his work with Morgenstern on utility, through Nash's equilibrium existence proof and Shapley's value and stochastic games, to Harsanyi's types for incomplete information, Aumann's correlated equilibrium and common knowledge, Selten's refinements for sequential play, and the folk theorem tradition in repeated games. A second lineage is algorithmic and comes from artificial intelligence and distributed systems: constraint satisfaction, asynchronous search, and dynamic programming, joined to the economic design tradition of Vickrey, Clarke, and Groves and to Arrow's social choice impossibility. The book's genealogy is deliberately dual: classical results are restated beside the algorithms that compute them, so every solution concept arrives with both a justification and a computational price.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model the reader as someone who will build systems of agents, not only admire theorems. Their working assumption is that self interest is the default, that rationality is a modeling tool rather than a description of people, and that any concept worth using must survive three questions: what exactly is defined, what can be computed, and what breaks when assumptions are relaxed. They repeatedly distrust intuition until it is formalized, prefer the weakest assumption that still yields a result, and treat examples as instruments for exposing where a definition is too strong or too weak. Their model of the domain is pluralistic: no single solution concept governs, and choosing among equilibrium, stability, fairness, and learnability criteria is itself part of the analyst's job.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto conclusions drawn elsewhere in an engine. Subgame perfection vetoes any plan whose optimality depends on a threat that is irrational at the node where it must be executed. Impossibility results veto aggregation rules that claim to be simultaneously efficient, independent, and nondictatorial. The core vetoes credit divisions that underpay any coalition below its standalone worth. Dominance vetoes recommendations that lose to an alternative against every opponent response. The folk theorem vetoes confident unique predictions in indefinitely repeated interactions, where many payoffs are sustainable. Together these act as a constraint layer: a forecast that fails any applicable veto is not merely unlikely, it is incoherent under the stated assumptions, and the engine must either repair it or disclose the assumption it abandons.

universal_lens: Any system of autonomous actors, from robots to firms to models in an ensemble, can be analyzed with the same sequence: write the interaction as a game, state each actor's information as partitions or types, test candidate outcomes for efficiency, best response stability, dominance, and credibility in subgames, ask which learning dynamic the actors are actually running, and only then aggregate or divide outcomes under declared fairness axioms. The template travels because it separates the questions that are often conflated: what is feasible, what is stable, what is learnable, and what is fair are four different properties, and a system that cannot say which one it has established does not understand its own prediction.
gsi_mapping: The Institute takes the book as curriculum backbone for multi actor reasoning: normal and extensive forms as the grammar of interaction, Bayesian types and partition models as the grammar of information, the folk theorem and replicator dynamic as the grammar of adaptation over time, and mechanism design as the grammar of building environments where honest reporting is optimal. It also takes the book's discipline of paired statements, every concept with its computability and its failure conditions, as the standard for how institute research notes must be written before a result is admitted to the shared corpus.
gse_mapping: The engine takes concrete machinery: matchup models as normal and stochastic games with equilibrium checks, tendency estimation as fictitious play with stationarity diagnostics, opponent modeling through Bayesian types updated from signals, credit assignment through Shapley marginal contributions audited against core inequalities, component pricing through VCG externality, aggregation of signal families under a declared Arrow relaxation, and subgame credibility vetoes on any game plan reasoning. Each module inherits the book's assumptions as runtime checks on live telemetry, so a conclusion is emitted only with the regime that licenses it.
